newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU farm ministers to attack beef label plans.
newsitem.headline: EU farm ministers to attack beef label plans.

text.p: European Union farm ministers are expected on Monday to fight a proposal making it compulsory to state the origin of beef, even though the move is aimed at reassuring consumers after the mad cow disease health scare.

Pressure to improve food safety rose last week after a European Commission report revealed widespread failures among EU member states to detect and eradicate the fatal brain wasting disease known as bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE).

But EU diplomats said ministers were angry that European Commission President Jacques Santer last month yielded to European Parliament demands for more power and given it a joint say on EU cattle identification and beef labelling systems.
"Most ministers are irritated and ready to let off a lot of steam," one diplomat said, adding that the proposal could now be delayed months by the need for extra parliamentary discussions.
Britain, Ireland and Italy are also objecting to a revised proposal by the EU Commission, aimed at satisfying parliamentary demands, making beef labels compulsory from January 2000.
The three countries claim this would stir nationalist sentiment and create a barrier to trade in the single EU market.
Although the proposed beef label would not specifiy the country of origin, it would give the regions in which cattle were born, fattened and slaughtered as well as feeding data.
Germany, Austria and France, as well as the European Parliament, however want additional compulsory information on the label to protect consumers.
"There's a big cleavage on labelling," one diplomat noted.

But the diplomat added that the gap had been narrowed on cattle identification. Member states were close to agreement on setting up an EU-wide network involving national computerised data bases and passports for each animal so that their movements can be traced from birth.

On Monday, the Dutch EU Presidency will try to make progress by seeing if there is the necessary unanimous agreement to reject the Commission's proposal and possibly adopt only the cattle identification scheme while just consulting parliament.

British agriculture minister Douglas Hogg is also expected to press for a first step in lifting a worldwide ban on British beef exports saying that Britain has now fulfilled all the pre- conditions agreed at the Florence EU summit in June 1995.
The ban was imposed a year ago after the British governent triggered a massive public health scare after admitting that BSE could be transmitted to humans who ate infected beef.
Nearly all the reported cases of BSE have been in Britain.

Hogg will urge that a reorganistion of the EU's food safety services should not serve as an excuse for delay and exports should soon be allowed from Northern Irish and other British herds certified to be free of BSE, British officials said.

But EU diplomats and officials said that any easing of the ban was still months away -- after the British general election due in May -- as the British reports and plans must first be studied by EU scientific committees.

They noted that allegations last week by British meat inspectors that London ignored warnings about meat safety despite a recent food poisoning outbreak in Scotland which killed 20 people, had made it more difficult to relax the ban.
